clue.text: South Americans sound in need of a warm-up

indicators.note: 'sound' asks for the words to be heard rather than read, so a spoken phrase stands for the spelling

blocks.note: people in need of a warm-up are cold ones, chilly 'uns in casual speech

explanation.surface: A group of South American visitors shivering and wanting a warm drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uns is the colloquial clipped form of ones; say 'chilly 'uns' quickly and it matches the nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of Chile, a country on the Pacific coast of South America, are Chileans.

clue.text: You once appeared in stockings in the nursery, perhaps

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside, wrapped by the outer word

blocks.note: hose is an old word for stockings or tights
thou is the archaic form of you

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned figure turning up wearing stockings in a child's nursery.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery is a plant nursery, not a children's room, which is why the setter adds 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: A heated glasshouse for raising tender plants is one kind of garden nursery, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Bard's loss?

blocks.note: surface reading: something Shakespeare lost
setter's reading: Shakespeare wrote a comedy titled Love's Labour's Lost, so the thing lost is a task undertaken for affection

explanation.walkthrough: The Bard is Shakespeare; turn round the title of his play and the lost thing is work done for nothing but fondness.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means work undertaken gladly without payment, echoing the item lost in Shakespeare's comedy title.

clue.text: Theoretical student of Plato at the university

definitions.text: student of Plato at the university

blocks.note: first meaning: concerned with theory rather than practice

blocks.clueFragment: student of Plato at the university
blocks.note: second meaning: a follower of Plato's school, the Academy, or anyone studying at a university

explanation.surface: A scholar of Plato at university with a head full of abstractions.
explanation.walkthrough: Plato taught at the Academy in Athens, so his pupils were literally academics.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means abstract or unpractical; the noun names a scholar, originally a member of Plato's Athenian school.

clue.text: The last possibility of secrecy

indicators.note: a possibility is one of several ways things might be, so these letters are taken in another possible arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Discretion as the final remaining option when everything else has failed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last possibility' reads as one phrase meaning a final resort; split it into fodder and indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealth is furtive, covert action, done quietly so as to avoid notice.

clue.text: Brown one of this author's colours, we hear?

indicators.note: 'we hear' signals that a word is heard, so the spelling follows the sound

blocks.note: hues are colours or shades

explanation.surface: Asking whether brown is among a writer's favourite colours.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown is Tom Brown, hero of Tom Brown's Schooldays by Thomas Hughes, so 'Brown one of this author's' identifies the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hughes was the Victorian novelist who created the schoolboy Tom Brown.

clue.text: Willingly and all that

definitions.note: a phrase defining a phrase: split into two words, the answer is the idiom that ends a list, fair because the enumeration (4) hides the space

blocks.note: first meaning: readily
second meaning, split into two words

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into two words for the second meaning; the first is the sense in 'I'd sooner stay'.
explanation.definitionFit: In 'as soon' and 'sooner' the word expresses readiness or preference, and split it gives the phrase 'so on'.

clue.text: Swinger helps to pass the time

definitions.text: Swinger helps to pass the time

blocks.clueFragment: Swinger helps to pass the time
blocks.note: surface reading: a lively partygoer helping to while away the hours

blocks.clueFragment: Swinger helps to pass the time
blocks.note: setter's reading: a weight swinging to and fro regulates a clock, marking the passing seconds

explanation.walkthrough: 'Swinger' suggests a fun-loving person, but it is something that literally swings inside a clock.
explanation.definitionFit: A weight hung on a rod that swings regularly, used to keep time in a long-case clock.

clue.text: Sweetheart kept on sending Christmas presents

blocks.note: first meaning: a beloved partner
second meaning: the giver in the carol The Twelve Days of Christmas, who sends a new gift every day

explanation.walkthrough: In the carol each verse begins 'On the first day of Christmas my ___ sent to me', and the gifts never stop.
explanation.definitionFit: The carol's giver is a devoted lover, and a sweetheart is someone's dearly beloved partner.

clue.text: Mad to reverse, try going forward

indicators.note: to reverse is to go backwards, so the letters of the word for mad are read from the end

blocks.note: bats is informal for crazy, as in 'gone bats'

explanation.surface: A driver who is told reversing would be crazy and to push on ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going forward' contrasts with the reversal: the definition is read normally.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the idiom of having a go: an attempt or shot at something, as in 'have a stab at it'.

clue.text: Antiquated drink

blocks.note: first meaning: out of date
second meaning: a whisky cocktail with bitters and sugar

explanation.surface: An outdated beverage nobody orders any more.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means behind the times; it is also the name of a classic bourbon cocktail with bitters.

clue.text: Drinks at Glyndebourne? They help one see stars

blocks.note: first meaning, whimsically: glasses drunk at an opera house
second meaning: small binoculars for watching the singers on stage

explanation.surface: Interval drinks at a country opera festival, then peering at the celebrated singers.
explanation.walkthrough: Glyndebourne is an opera festival in an English country house, famous for picnics and interval champagne. The stars are the singers, not the night sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Small binoculars used by audiences to get a close view of performers on a theatre stage.

clue.text: What you give a quid for — drink for enough people

blocks.clueFragment: What you give a quid for
blocks.note: in the Latin phrase quid pro quo, the quid is given in return for the quo
rum is a spirit

explanation.surface: Paying a pound for a round of drinks for a large enough crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: A quid is British slang for a pound, which pulls the reader towards money; here it is the Latin 'something' in quid pro quo.
explanation.definitionFit: The minimum number of members who must be present for a meeting's decisions to be valid.

clue.text: Refined suet fat changes many -

indicators.note: a thing that changes takes a different form, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a crossword stand-in for many

explanation.surface: Genteel cooking alters a great deal about suet fat.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing good judgement about style and quality, elegant and cultivated rather than vulgar.

clue.text: Unqualified, to be exact

blocks.note: first meaning: absolute, utter, as in a total stranger
second meaning: precise, flawless in accuracy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Unqualified' suggests lacking credentials, but here it means without reservation.
explanation.definitionFit: As in 'a perfect stranger' the word means utter or absolute; it also means precisely accurate, as in a perfect copy.

clue.text: -What a state we were in before our first appearance!

definitions.text: What a state we were in before our first appearance!

blocks.clueFragment: What a state we were in before our first appearance!
blocks.note: surface reading: performers in a panic before their debut on stage

blocks.clueFragment: What a state we were in before our first appearance!
blocks.note: setter's reading: the condition everyone was in before being born, our first appearance in the world

explanation.walkthrough: 'What a state' sounds like nerves, but the state is literal: the condition before birth.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes the period before birth, when a baby is still developing in the womb.

clue.text: Would a hair-cut have-saved- Davidson?

blocks.note: surface reading: wondering whether a trim would have rescued a man called Davidson
setter's reading: King David's son in the Bible was caught by his long hair in an oak tree and killed

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Davidson' as David's son: in 2 Samuel the rebel prince's hair snagged in a tree as he fled, leaving him hanging for Joab to kill.
explanation.definitionFit: The rebellious third son of King David, whose long hair trapped him in an oak tree.

clue.text: Dutch flier of birds

blocks.note: a bat is a flying mammal
avian means relating to birds

explanation.surface: A Dutch pilot, or a Dutch bird-fancier's pigeon.
explanation.walkthrough: Batavia was the Latin name for the Netherlands region, after the Batavi tribe.
explanation.definitionFit: Batavian is a literary adjective for Dutch, from the Batavi, an ancient Germanic tribe of the Rhine delta.

clue.text: Master's about arrived

definitions.note: read as 'mastered'; the answer is past tense

blocks.note: over means about, as in arguing over money
came is the past tense of come, to arrive

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster's whereabouts: he has just turned up.
explanation.definitionFit: To get the better of or conquer something is to master it, so defeated or conquered fits.

clue.text: Helps invalid — perhaps does some cooking

blocks.note: first meaning: gives medical treatment to a sick person
second meaning: falsifies or tampers with, as in cooking the books

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooking' is the slang sense of falsifying accounts, not preparing food.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means both treating a patient medically and tampering with figures or evidence.

clue.text: Old age, or trouble in get-rich quick land

blocks.note: eld is an archaic word for old age
taken as written
ado is fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: Choosing between growing old or hardship in a land of instant fortunes.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary city of gold sought by Spanish conquistadors, now any place offering fast riches.

clue.text: Silver-topped item under the hammer? A bit of finger trouble

indicators.note: in a down entry, being topped by something means it sits above, so the first piece comes first

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a nail is what a hammer strikes, not an auction lot

explanation.surface: A silver-capped lot at auction, then a minor problem with a finger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under the hammer' normally means up for auction; here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Another name for a hangnail, a painful torn sliver of skin beside a fingernail.

clue.text: Row about officer as a quixotic fighter

indicators.note: one word placed about another goes around it, enclosing it

blocks.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
Lt is the abbreviation for lieutenant

explanation.surface: A quarrel involving an officer who fights like Don Quixote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' rhymes with cow (a quarrel) in the surface but rhymes with go (a line) in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: One who tilts, jousting with a lance, as Don Quixote famously charged at windmills.

clue.text: Adapt oysters for other courses

blocks.note: to alter is to adapt or modify
natives are oysters raised in British beds, especially at Whitstable

explanation.surface: A chef adapting an oyster dish for different courses of a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courses' suggests a menu, but means courses of action.
explanation.definitionFit: Options or choices available instead of the present plan are different courses of action.

clue.text: Kiddie has -a point to convey

blocks.note: a tot is a small child
E is east, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A small child has a point to get across.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry or haul something from one place to another, informally, as in toting a bag.

clue.text: See — bottoms, one might argue?

definitions.note: plural phrase for a singular noun

blocks.note: first meaning: a bishop's see is the place of his throne, his official base
second meaning: the backside, which some would say is what people sit on

explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is not the verb: a see is a bishop's diocese, whose centre is the cathedral throne.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop's official seat is his see, and one's seat is a polite word for one's backside.

clue.text: Prior upset, riot near

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A monastery's prior is distressed by a disturbance close by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prior' looks like the head of a priory, but it is the adjective meaning earlier.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something coming earlier in time or order, preceding another.

clue.text: Lays thrice (in combinations), this bird

blocks.note: a lay is a song or ballad
ter- is the Latin prefix for three times, used in compound words

explanation.surface: A bird singing its tunes three times over, in different arrangements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lays' suggests eggs, which fits the bird, but the lays are ballads.
explanation.definitionFit: A singing bird such as a thrush or warbler is a songbird, noted for its musical calls.
